text: Rusting, its prevention, and iron from its ore

md: Leave a bike out all winter and the chain goes orange and flaky. Leave the same bike in a dry shed and it does not. Rusting is a chemical reaction with two ingredients, and knowing which two is enough to stop it — which matters, because we make bridges, ships and railways out of the metal it eats.

prompt: Read the picture. Iron rusts when it meets which two things?
explain: Water and oxygen, both at once. The rest of the lesson is about proving that and then using it.

alt: A heavily rusted steel bolt lying on gravel, its whole surface covered in flaky orange-brown rust with the shape of the head almost lost
caption: Rust is not a stain: it is a flaky new solid, and it falls off to leave fresh iron exposed underneath.
prompt: Give the chemical name of the orange-brown solid, in full. Why does rust keep eating into an object instead of sealing it, the way aluminium's oxide layer does?

md: Rust is **hydrated iron(III) oxide**. Both halves of that name carry a mark. **Hydrated** says the water is built into the solid, which is why rust needs water and not just air; **iron(III)** says which of iron's two oxides it is. Rust is also **flaky**, so it falls away and leaves fresh iron exposed — which is why an iron object rusts right through, given time.

explain: Hydrated. Leaving that word out is the single commonest way to lose half the marks on this question.

md:
**The question.** Four stoppered tubes are left for a week. Which nails rust, and why?
**Step 1 — find the control.** Tube A has a nail in ordinary tap water with air above it. Both ingredients are there, so it rusts, and it shows the others what a normal result looks like.
**Step 2 — read tube B.** The anhydrous calcium chloride is a **drying agent**: it removes the water from the air in the tube. No water, no rust.

prompt: What is the anhydrous calcium chloride in tube B for?
options: it removes the water from the air
it stops water getting into the tube
it removes the oxygen from the air
answer: it removes the water from the air
explain: It absorbs water that is already there. 'Stops water getting in' is the answer CCEA does not credit, because the bung already does that.

md:
**Step 3 — read tube C.** The water was boiled first, which drives the dissolved air out of it, and the oil layer then stops oxygen **dissolving back in**. No oxygen, no rust.
**Step 4 — read tube D.** Salty water has both ingredients and rusts fastest of all, which is why cars rust sooner near the sea. Conclusion: rusting needs water **and** oxygen together.

prompt: What is the layer of oil in tube C for?
options: it stops oxygen dissolving back into the water
answer: it stops oxygen dissolving back into the water
explain: Say the word dissolving. 'To keep oxygen out' on its own is recorded as not detailed enough for the mark.

md:
The simplest defence is a **barrier** between the iron and the air: **painting**, **oiling or greasing**, **plastic coating**, or **galvanising**, which is coating the iron with **zinc**. Each keeps water and oxygen off the metal.
Name them carefully. 'Plastic' and 'metal' on their own are not accepted — the answer is plastic **coating** and metal **coating**, because it is the coating, not the material, that does the work.

alt: An extreme close-up of a hot-dip galvanised steel surface, showing the interlocking crystal spangle pattern of the zinc layer in grey with a faint bluish sheen
caption: The surface of galvanised steel, close up. Those interlocking crystals are the zinc layer, and they are what you are naming when you say galvanising.
prompt: Which metal is this layer made of? Give two separate reasons why it protects the steel underneath — one that works while it is intact, and one that keeps working after it is scratched.

title: GCSE Chemistry - What is Corrosion and How to Stop it (2026/27 exams)
why: The barrier methods run past in order, with what each one is good for.

prompt: Galvanising means coating iron with which metal?
explain: Zinc. Examiners record candidates who know the word galvanising but never say which metal is involved, and the metal is the mark.

md: A barrier fails as soon as it is scratched. **Sacrificial protection** does not. Bolt a block of a **more reactive metal** — zinc or magnesium — onto the iron and that metal gives up its electrons first, so it corrodes instead of the iron. That is why galvanising beats the other barriers: the zinc is a barrier **and** a sacrifice.

title: Why it has to be a more reactive metal
md: Reactivity is the tendency to give up electrons. Put zinc against iron and the zinc gives its electrons up more readily, so the zinc corrodes and the iron is left alone. A metal **below** iron, such as tin, does the opposite: scratch a tin can and the iron corrodes faster.

alt: The underside of a boat's steel hull out of the water, with a pale grey oval block of zinc bolted flat against the black-painted plating near the propeller shaft
caption: A real sacrificial block, bolted to a hull near the propeller. It is inspected and replaced when it has corroded away.
prompt: Name the metal the pale block is likely to be, and explain in two steps why it protects the steel. Why must it be replaced from time to time?
Why does a block of magnesium bolted to a steel pipeline stop the pipeline rusting?
options: magnesium is more reactive, so it corrodes instead of the iron
magnesium is less reactive, so it protects the iron
magnesium seals the pipeline so no water reaches it
answer: magnesium is more reactive, so it corrodes instead of the iron
explain: More reactive, so it gives up its electrons first. A single bolted-on block cannot seal a whole pipeline, so a barrier is not the explanation here.

md:
Iron is extracted from **haematite**, an ore containing iron(III) oxide, in a **blast furnace**. Three solids are tipped in at the top — haematite, **coke** (carbon) and **limestone** — and **hot air** is blasted in near the base.
The iron comes out as a liquid at the bottom, with a second liquid, the **slag**, floating on top of it. The two are tapped off through separate holes, slag above iron.

prompt: The ore that iron is extracted from is called ______.
explain: Haematite. Bauxite is the ore of aluminium, and confusing the two is a recorded error.

md:
Four reactions, in order.
**Burning the coke:** $\ce{C + O2 -> CO2}$, which supplies the heat.
**Making the reducing agent (Higher):** $\ce{CO2 + C -> 2CO}$.
**Reducing the ore:** $\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}$ — the carbon monoxide takes the oxygen away.
**Removing the acidic impurities (Higher):** the limestone decomposes, $\ce{CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2}$, and the basic calcium oxide then takes out the acidic sand as slag: $\ce{CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3}$.

alt: Two labelled boxes joined by an arrow carrying two electrons: the reducing agent gives electrons away and is oxidised, the oxidising agent takes them and is reduced.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 296" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="cagt"><title id="cagt">Two boxes: the reducing agent gives electrons away and is itself oxidised, while the oxidising agent takes electrons and is itself reduced</title><defs><marker id="cag" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z" fill="currentColor"/></marker></defs><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.7"><rect x="40" y="90" width="270" height="110" rx="8"/><rect x="390" y="90" width="270" height="110" rx="8"/></g><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4"><path d="M318 134 H382" marker-end="url(#cag)"/></g><g fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="1" stroke="none"><circle cx="336" cy="116" r="5"/><circle cx="356" cy="116" r="5"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle"><text x="175" y="126" font-size="15" font-weight="600">reducing agent</text><text x="175" y="154">gives electrons away</text><text x="175" y="180">so it is oxidised itself</text><text x="525" y="126" font-size="15" font-weight="600">oxidising agent</text><text x="525" y="154">takes electrons</text><text x="525" y="180">so it is reduced itself</text><text x="350" y="104" font-size="11.5">electrons</text></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="24" y="34" font-size="13" font-weight="600">Which one is the agent?</text><text x="24" y="54" font-size="11.5">The two filled circles on the arrow are electrons moving from left to right.</text><text x="24" y="240" font-size="11.5">In the blast furnace the carbon monoxide is the reducing agent: it takes the oxygen off the</text><text x="24" y="258" font-size="11.5">iron(III) oxide, and is itself oxidised to carbon dioxide while doing it.</text></g></svg>
caption: Carbon monoxide does to the ore exactly what the reducing agent does in the picture.

prompt: Which substance actually takes the oxygen away from the iron(III) oxide?
explain: Carbon monoxide is the reducing agent, which is why the furnace goes to the trouble of making it from carbon dioxide and coke first.

md:
Name rust in full, with both marking words.
Explain what every tube in the conditions experiment shows, and what the oil and the drying agent are for.
List the barrier methods, qualified as coatings, and say what galvanising is.
Explain sacrificial protection using the reactivity series.
Name the raw materials of the blast furnace and write its four equations.

Rusting and redox usually share one C2 question, around nine marks. The name of rust is **[2]**, one mark for *hydrated* and one for *iron(III) oxide*. Apparatus purposes are **[1]** each, with tight accept lists. Galvanising is **[2]**: coated in zinc, then the reason. Furnace equations are marked in three parts, and slag is tapped off **above** the molten iron.
